content: Removing dental plaque is essential for maintaining oral health. There has been ongoing debate regarding the effectiveness of manual versus powered toothbrushes in achieving this goal. This study is an updated Cochrane review, originally published in 2003 and updated in 2005, that aims to compare the two types of toothbrushes in terms of plaque removal, gingival health, staining, calculus, reliability, adverse effects, and cost. The review included randomized controlled trials lasting at least four weeks, comparing unsupervised use of powered toothbrushes with manual toothbrushes in both children and adults. A comprehensive search of multiple electronic databases was conducted, including the Cochrane Oral Health Group's Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL, up to January 23, 2014. No restrictions were placed on language or publication date. Ongoing trials were also identified through the US National Institutes of Health Trials Register and the WHO Clinical Trials Registry Platform. A total of 56 trials met the inclusion criteria, with 51 trials involving 4624 participants providing data for meta-analysis. Five trials were assessed as having a low risk of bias, five as high risk, and 46 as unclear risk. The data were analyzed using random-effects models when four or more studies were included in the meta-analysis; otherwise, fixed-effect models were used. Outcomes were categorized as short-term (1 to 3 months) or long-term (greater than 3 months). The results showed moderate-quality evidence that powered toothbrushes significantly reduced plaque compared to manual toothbrushes. In the short term, powered toothbrushes achieved a standardized mean difference (SMD) of -0.50 (95% confidence interval [CI]: -0.70 to -0.31) based on 40 trials with 2871 participants. In the long term, the SMD was -0.47 (95% CI: -0.82 to -0.11) based on 14 trials with 978 participants. These findings correspond to an 11% reduction in plaque in the short term and a 21% reduction in the long term, as measured by the Quigley Hein index (Turesky). However, both meta-analyses exhibited high heterogeneity (I² = 83% and 86%, respectively), which could not be explained by the different types of powered toothbrushes. For gingivitis, powered toothbrushes also demonstrated a statistically significant benefit over manual toothbrushes. In the short term, the SMD was -0.43 (95% CI: -0.60 to -0.25) based on 44 trials with 3345 participants. In the long term, the SMD was -0.21 (95% CI: -0.31 to -0.12) based on 16 trials with 1645 participants. These results correspond to a 6% reduction in gingivitis in the short term and an 11% reduction in the long term, as measured by the Löe and Silness index. Again, high heterogeneity was observed in the meta-analyses (I² = 82% and 51%, respectively), which was not explained by the different types of powered toothbrushes. The trials included various types of powered toothbrushes: side-to-side (10 trials), counter-oscillation (5 trials), rotation-oscillation (27 trials), circular (2 trials), ultrasonic (7 trials), ionic (4 trials), and unknown types (5 trials). The rotation-oscillation brushes had the most substantial evidence base and showed statistically significant reductions in both plaque and gingivitis at both time points. The authors concluded that powered toothbrushes are more effective than manual toothbrushes in reducing plaque and gingivitis in both the short and long term. However, the clinical significance of these findings remains uncertain. Future trials and meta-analyses would benefit from adherence to methodological guidelines and greater standardization in study design. Cost, reliability, and side effects were inconsistently reported across the studies. Any reported side effects were localized and temporary.
